turns.doctor_question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I’m here because... I mean, honestly, it’s about my house, but everyone keeps acting like this foreclosure is just, you know, standard paperwork and missed payments. Like it's just some normal financial mistake or a clerical thing. But it’s not. I supervise the sales floor at my retail job, so I know how to track things, I know how to spot when things don't add up, and I have been watching this happen for almost two years now. Two whole years. 

And I know for an absolute fact that the bank, the loan servicer, and even people at my job—which I know sounds strange to people who aren't paying attention, but I am—they have all been quietly working together to push me out of my house. They coordinate it behind my back. People just look at the mail and say, 'Oh, it's just a late notice,' but they don't see the whole picture. They don't see how the dates on the bank letters line up exactly with when my coworkers start acting weird around me or whispering when I come into the breakroom. 

It's a whole orchestrated thing to force me out of my home, and no amount of papers they show me, no matter how official they make these foreclosure documents look with their stamps and their legal jargon, changes what I’ve been seeing with my own two eyes for the last twenty-something months. They just want me out, and they're all in on it together, and no one will just sit down and look at what is actually happening to me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, persecutory belief that their bank, loan servicer, and coworkers are conspiring to force them out of their home, and states that no evidence or paperwork will change their mind.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually energized or high and needed much less sleep?
turns.patient_response:
Energized? Like... high? No, I mean, I don't know why you'd ask that. I certainly don't feel great about any of this. If I'm not sleeping, it's definitely not because I have some kind of boundless energy or feel unusually good. It's because I'm exhausted, but I have to stay vigilant. You try sleeping when you know there's a coordinated effort to steal your house. 

I mean, I'm up at 2 AM sometimes, sure, but I'm sitting at my kitchen table, going through the mail with a yellow highlighter, trying to cross-reference the postmarks on the bank envelopes with the exact days my manager schedules me for closing shifts. Because I noticed a pattern—they always seem to time the delivery of these so-called 'default notices' for the nights I'm too tired from closing the sales floor to properly analyze them. It's completely calculated. 

So, no, I don't feel high. I feel drained. I want to sleep. I really do. I bought blackout curtains, I drink chamomile tea, I do all the things you're supposed to do to wind down, but how can you actually rest when you know the minute you close your eyes, the people who are supposed to be ringing up customers at your job are probably texting the loan servicer to give them updates on my schedule? If I'm awake and getting less sleep, it's purely out of necessity. It's survival. I'm just trying to keep a roof over my head while everyone else is playing these games, so no, no extra energy here. Just a lot of stress.

turns.doctor_question: Have you heard voices when no one else was there?
turns.patient_response:
Voices? Like, hearing things that aren't there? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, I know why you're asking that, I've seen the movies, but no. My hearing is perfectly fine, and I only hear what people are actually saying. 

The problem isn't that I'm hearing imaginary voices, the problem is what I'm hearing real people say when they think I'm not listening. Like, just last Tuesday, I was in the stockroom—I'm the supervisor, so I do the inventory checks, right?—and I heard two of the cashiers whispering on the other side of the shelving unit. They didn't know I was there. And they were talking about 'the timeline.' That's the exact phrase they used: 'the timeline.' Now, why would two part-time cashiers be talking about a timeline unless they were referring to the bank's timeline for my house? They were whispering, but I heard them clear as day. 

And then, when I walked around the corner, they completely stopped talking. Just dead silence. And one of them—Sarah, who just started three months ago—she looked at her phone and then looked at me with this really specific expression. So, no, I don't hear voices in my head. I hear the very real conversations that my coworkers are having about me and my property. I hear the loan servicer on the phone when I call them, talking in circles, using all this jargon to confuse me, but their tone of voice tells me everything I need to know. They get this smug, condescending tone, like they know something I don't, like they know the trap is already set. 

So, no, no hallucinations. No voices from the walls or anything crazy like that. I'm completely grounded in reality. I just have very good ears, and I pay attention to the things people say when they think I'm out of earshot. That's how I know they're all working together. You don't need to hear imaginary voices when the real ones are conspiring against you right out in the open, if you just know how to listen.

turns.doctor_question: Has anyone told you that your speech or your thoughts seem hard to follow or jumbled?
turns.patient_response:
Jumbled? No, I mean, no one has ever said that to me. If anything, I think I'm probably too clear for them. That's the issue, isn't it? When you start putting the pieces together and you can articulate exactly how the bank is coordinating with the scheduling manager to exhaust you so you miss the fine print on the default notices... people don't like that. They don't want you to be clear. 

So no, nobody says I'm hard to follow. Sometimes my sister will say, 'You're overthinking this,' or 'You're talking too fast,' but that's just because she doesn't want to hear it. She doesn't want to admit that the situation is as bad as it is. It's much easier for her to just pretend everything is fine and that I'm just stressed about work. But my thoughts aren't jumbled at all. I have them all written out, actually. I have a whole notebook where I track the shifts, the mail deliveries, the phone calls. It's incredibly organized. It has to be. If my thoughts were jumbled, I would have lost the house months ago. 

I mean, just look at how I manage the store. You can't be a supervisor and have jumbled thoughts. I handle the inventory, I handle the cash drops, I manage a team of six people—even if two of them are clearly feeding information to the loan servicer. I still manage them effectively. You have to be sharp. You have to be ten steps ahead. So if someone were to say my thoughts were hard to follow, it would just be a tactic. It would just be another way to discredit me so that when I finally take all this evidence to a lawyer, they'll say, 'Oh, don't listen to her, she's confused.' But I'm not confused. I know exactly what's happening.

turns.doctor_question: Has anything happened that made you believe people can control your thoughts or put thoughts into your mind?
turns.patient_response:
Control my thoughts? Put thoughts in my mind? No, no, of course not. That sounds like something out of a science fiction movie. My thoughts are completely my own, and honestly, my mind is the one thing I have absolute control over right now. If the bank or the loan servicer could just magically put thoughts into my head, don't you think they would have done it by now? They would have just planted a thought like, 'Oh, this is all too hard, I should just let them foreclose,' or 'I should just sign this modification paperwork without reading the addendum.' 

But they can't do that. They can't get inside my head like that. What they do try to do, though, is influence my thinking through exhaustion and stress. Like the scheduling manager at work? He’s been giving me these back-to-back closing and opening shifts—we call them 'clopens' in retail—and I know exactly why he's doing it. He's doing it to wear me down physically so that my resolve weakens. They figure if I'm tired enough, I'll make a mistake, or I'll just get so overwhelmed that I'll surrender the property. They leave the inventory logs a complete mess on purpose so I have to stay an hour past my shift fixing them, which cuts into the time I have at home to review my case files and track the discrepancies in my escrow account. 

So they use psychological pressure, absolutely. They use manipulation, they use surveillance—like Sarah and the others watching me—but they do not control my actual thoughts. I am incredibly protective of my mental space. I don't even listen to the radio on my commute anymore. I drive in total silence for twenty-five minutes just so I can review my strategy for the day, step by step, without any distractions. I know exactly what I think and why I think it. My mind is my armor in all of this. It's the one thing they can't touch, and frankly, I think that's why they are escalating things at the store. They're frustrated because I'm still thinking for myself and I'm still ten steps ahead of them. So no, nobody is putting thoughts in my mind. I wouldn't let them even if it were possible.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly describes persecutory delusions, believing that their scheduling manager, coworkers, and the bank are conspiring against them, surveilling them, and intentionally trying to wear them down to take their property.

turns.doctor_question: Have you become less interested in seeing friends or doing things you used to enjoy?
turns.patient_response:
Less interested? No, not at all. I mean, I still want to do the things I love, I just literally do not have the luxury of free time right now. There's a huge difference. 

Like, I used to go out with my friends Melissa and Jen every other Friday. We’d go get margaritas and do the trivia night down at this pub near the mall. I love trivia. I’m usually the one who carries the team on the history and geography questions. I haven't lost interest in that, I still really want to go! But, I mean, how can I sit there and try to remember the capital of North Dakota when I know for a fact that the bank is actively trying to push through a fraudulent default notice on my house? I can't just turn my brain off and drink a margarita when I have deadlines to meet and documents to review. Plus, they don't really get it. Melissa just tells me to 'take a breath' and 'let the lawyers handle it,' which just shows how naive she is about how these servicers operate. So I haven't lost interest in my friends, it's just hard to relate to them when they refuse to see what's right in front of them.

And it's the exact same thing with my hobbies. I have this garden out back, and I planted these incredible heirloom tomatoes in the spring—Cherokee Purples, they're my absolute favorite, they get this amazing dark color and they taste incredible. I love being out there in the dirt, it's usually so relaxing. I really miss it. But by the time I get home from one of those exhausting 'clopen' shifts I told you about, and then I have to spend three hours cross-referencing my certified mail receipts with the postal service tracking database to prove they're withholding my correspondence... it's pitch black outside. And I can't exactly go out into the yard with a flashlight at midnight. That just draws attention to the house, and I know for a fact they have people driving by to check on my occupancy status to try and claim the property is abandoned. 

So, no, my interests haven't changed. I'm not sitting around depressed or apathetic, if that's what you're getting at. I have zero lack of interest in my life. It's strictly a matter of prioritization. When your entire livelihood and your property are under a coordinated attack, you have to put the fun stuff on the back burner. It's just survival. If I had my way, I'd be out in the garden every single evening, but they've made absolutely sure I don't have that option right now.

Intensely sad? Hopeless? No. No, not at all. I mean, I'm angry, sure. I'm incredibly frustrated, absolutely. But hopeless? Did I sit in my car and cry about it? Did I feel sad? No! I marched right in there, got the printout, had them time-stamp it, and put it straight into Binder Number 4. That’s my correspondence binder. I have five of them now, all color-coded. You don't build five binders of meticulously cross-referenced evidence if you're feeling hopeless. 

So, no, no two weeks of intense sadness. I literally do not have the luxury of being sad. Sadness requires downtime. Sadness means you're sitting around wallowing, and I am way too busy defending my property and my livelihood to sit around feeling sorry for myself. I have to be the strong one here. If I let myself get sad or mopey, my sister would just use it as an excuse to say, 'See, you're just depressed, you need to let the house go, you're not thinking straight.' And I am absolutely not giving her, or the bank, or my manager the satisfaction of seeing me break. So, no. Not sad, not hopeless. Just highly, highly motivated to expose all of this.

And the bank calls... it wasn't just one or two polite calls during normal business hours. It was relentless. They would call at 7:15 in the morning, they would call at 8:45 at night, trying to catch me off guard, trying to create this atmosphere of constant panic in my own home. You couldn't even sit down to eat dinner or try to relax for five minutes without the phone ringing. And if you didn't answer, they'd just call back three minutes later from a slightly different local area code to trick you into picking up. They use these VoIP spoofing programs, you know. 

It just completely hijacked my entire life. Before that year and nine month mark, I was just a normal person going to work, managing the floor at the store, coming home, maybe working in the garden like I told you. But ever since those notices started flooding in and the phone started ringing off the hook, it's been a second full-time job just defending myself from them. I've had to completely restructure my entire existence around protecting this house. So yes, way, way more than a month. It’s been twenty-one months of absolute, coordinated harassment, and they haven't let up for a single second.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed, elaborate belief of a coordinated conspiracy involving surveillance, fraudulent documents, and relentless harassment to take their house.

turns.doctor_question: Have people told you that your face or voice seems less expressive than it used to?
turns.patient_response:
Less expressive? Like... blank? No. No, definitely not. I mean, if anything, people probably think I'm *too* expressive these days. You should hear me on the phone with the mortgage company. When I finally get a human being on the line after sitting on hold for forty-five minutes listening to that awful elevator jazz music they play—which, by the way, I'm completely convinced they loop intentionally just to break down your psychological resolve—I am extremely expressive. I have to be. I have to raise my voice and articulate every single syllable so they know I mean business. I don't let them talk over me. 

And at work? At the store, I'm the supervisor. I have to be "on" all the time. I have to smile at the customers, I have to direct my team, I have to look completely put-together and engaged. Because remember what I said about the invoices? They want me fired. They are looking for any excuse, any tiny slip-up. If I walk in there looking like a zombie, with a flat face, not talking to anyone or mumbling my words, my regional manager would be down my throat in a second. They'd write me up for "failing to maintain store morale" or some corporate garbage like that, and boom, I'm out of a job, and the bank swoops in. 

So I make a very conscious effort to be animated. I say "Good morning!" loud and clear. I ask the cashiers about their weekends. I project my voice across the floor when I'm directing the stock boys. I have to show them that I am sharp and completely aware of my surroundings. 

So no, nobody has said I'm less expressive. My sister did tell me I sound incredibly stressed out when I call her, and maybe my voice gets a little tight when I'm explaining the latest fraudulent letter I received in the mail, but being stressed isn't the same as being blank or emotionless. I'm fighting for my life here, doctor. You can't fight a battle like this with a blank face. You have to be loud. You have to make them hear you.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses clear persecutory delusions, believing that people at work want them fired, are looking for any excuse to do so, and that they are receiving fraudulent letters and fighting for their life.
symptom_reasoning.S023: The patient explicitly denies having diminished emotional expression, stating they are definitely not blank or less expressive, and in fact make a conscious effort to be animated and loud.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever felt that other people could hear your thoughts, as if your thoughts were not private?
turns.patient_response:
Hear my thoughts? Like... literally hear them? No. No, of course not. I mean, they are sophisticated, doctor. The people trying to take my house, the people at the bank, the ones slipping those fake invoices into my delivery manifests at the store—they are highly organized. They monitor my credit, they probably tap my phone line—actually, I'm almost certain they listen to my calls because there's always this faint clicking sound when I talk to my sister, and the volume drops out randomly. But reading my mind? Hearing my actual thoughts? No, that's... that's like science fiction. That's not how real-world corporate fraud works. 

If they could hear my thoughts, I would have lost the house months ago. Honestly, my thoughts are the only true advantage I have left in all of this! When I'm sitting at the kitchen table at 2:00 AM, looking at the pink and yellow highlighted folders, I formulate my counter-strategies in my head before I ever dare write them down. I know better than to speak my plans out loud in the house, just in case they've planted something, you know, a listening device or something when the gas meter guy came by last month. I didn't trust him for a second, by the way. He lingered way, way too long near the side window by the AC unit, and he wasn't even wearing a standard utility badge, just a generic clip-on. 

But my mind? No, my mind is a steel trap. It has to be. It's the one place they absolutely cannot get into. If they could hear what I was thinking, they'd know exactly which state regulatory agency I'm planning to report them to next, and they'd already have a fake paper trail ready to discredit me before I even mailed the certified letter. They'd know I figured out the discrepancy in the routing numbers on the escrow statement. So, no, my thoughts are completely private. They have to be. Keeping everything locked up right here in my head is literally the only way I can stay one step ahead of this whole operation. If I lose my privacy there, I lose everything. So no, nobody is hearing my thoughts.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies thought broadcasting but clearly demonstrates persecutory delusions, expressing fixed, elaborate beliefs that a highly organized group is trying to steal their house, tapping their phones, and planting listening devices.

turns.doctor_question: Since all this started, have you become unable to manage basic daily things like bathing, dressing, or keeping your home in order?
turns.patient_response:
Unable to manage? Like I'm just sitting around in dirty clothes staring at the wall? Oh, absolutely not. No, I mean, I told you earlier, I'm the supervisor. I have to be completely on top of things. 

When the whole... foreclosure situation isn't actively blowing up in my face, I function perfectly fine. I get up every single morning, I take my shower, I do my hair, I iron my work shirts—because you can't have wrinkles when you're managing a retail floor, it sets a terrible example for the younger staff—and I go to work. I supervise my team, I write up the weekly schedules, I handle all the customer issues, you know, the usual "I want to speak to a manager" complaints. I take care of myself. I keep my house clean, too. I mean, yes, my kitchen table is completely covered in my files, the yellow and pink and green folders I told you about, but the rest of the house is spotless. I vacuum every Sunday. 

The only time things get... well, derailed, I guess you could say, is when it connects back to the house. That's when the problems start. If the phone rings and it's that 1-800 number from the bank, or if I go out to the mailbox and there's another one of those thick, unmarked envelopes... well, obviously I have to stop whatever normal thing I was doing. If I was about to make dinner, dinner has to wait. Because I have to sit down right then and there, open the letter, get my highlighters out, and figure out what angle they're playing today. 

Or at work, if I'm right in the middle of doing the payroll or the schedules, and I notice a weird gap in the delivery paperwork, or an invoice that doesn't look right, I have to drop the schedule and investigate the paperwork immediately. Because I know that's them trying to trap me so they can get me fired. So it's not that I *can't* manage my basic daily life, doctor. I am incredibly capable. It's just that my daily routine gets hijacked by this massive, coordinated attack on my home and my livelihood. If they would just leave me alone and stop sending these fake documents, my days would be perfectly normal.
